transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Voting ends today, but one big question for Republicans is whether President Trump's
base from 2024 will turn out to vote in these midterms.
Some of the races being watched closely are Senate contests in Texas, Michigan, and Alaska,
and P.R.
has more.
NPR has been checking in with voters all year as part of a project called Swing Shift.
Wally and Gerald both live in Georgia and both voted for President Trump two years ago.
We agreed not to use their full name so they can speak freely about politics.
In this election, they've taken different paths.
Here's Gerald.
I just voted quick and easy, Republican, down the ballot, no split ticket here.
But Wally swung his vote to the Democrats.
We need wholesale change in this midterm, and we also need a big change for the next
presidential election.
Voters get the final say now.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Thirty-six states are holding gubernatorial contests.
Nineteen incumbents are leaving office.
NPR's Larry Kaplow reports that candidates who prevail in races for governor could play
a role in President Trump's future agenda.
Currently, 26 states are led by Republican governors, and many have used their power
to do things like increase local law enforcement cooperation with ICE or to provide voter
data to the Trump administration.
Some of the country's 24 Democratic governors have limited cooperation with ICE or joined
lawsuits that have helped block Trump tariffs or administration cuts in money for healthcare.
Some of the closest gubernatorial races are in Wisconsin and Kansas, where Democrats are
term-limited and Republicans have a chance to flip the office.
Democrats are eyeing opportunities to pick up governors' offices in states including
Nevada, Iowa, Georgia, and Ohio.
Larry Kaplow, NPR News.
U.S. funding for Israel has been a political flashpoint heading into these midterm elections.
NPR's Franco Ordonez reports President Trump now says the funding stops after this year.
Speaking to Fox News' Fox and Friends, the president said Israel no longer needed the
funding.
Now, as far as paying Israel, the BB Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel
$4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping.
It was not clear what specific funding Trump was referring to, a memorandum of understanding
that provides $3.8 billion in military aid was set to expire in 2028.
Trump also said that Israel can continue to buy whatever they want.
Asked about the timing of the announcement on election day, Trump said it wasn't a good
talking point, acknowledging that some Democrats were using the financial support to criticize
Republicans.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
This is NPR.
The head of Britain's cybersecurity is projecting artificial intelligence breaches on critical
infrastructure in the United Kingdom by 2028.
In a report out today, Richard Horn warns outdated technology exposes the region to
cyber attacks that could lead to severe disruptions to the public, such as power outages.
The National Cybersecurity Center highlights China's advanced cyber activity and Russia's
strategic campaigns among the security threats.
Six years since the onset of the COVID pandemic and work from home, many building owners are
still struggling to fill unused and expensive spaces.
But reporter Al Orendorf brings us the story of a Chicago entrepreneur who thinks he can
help solve the problem.
Russell Steinberg founded Farm Zero with a vision to repurpose empty high-rise office
space to grow and sell edible greens.
Hybrid work has left 30 percent of Chicago's downtown office space empty.
Steinberg believes indoor agriculture can help fill that revenue gap.
There was enough pain across the stakeholders in downtown office buildings that people were
willing to walk the line and get to the bottom of whether this could actually be done.
Steinberg says a lot of cities have asked about his urban farming idea, which he hopes
will help more downtown business districts recapture the bounty of their salad days.
For NPR News, I'm Al Orendorf in Chicago.
When he says its military has saved the crew of an Iranian fishing vessel that was hijacked
off Somalia over the weekend, it says there were no casualties.
This is NPR.

Thirty-six states hold gubernatorial races; Wisconsin and Kansas seen as closest contests
President Trump says U.S. stopping $4 billion yearly Israel funding, sparking midterm debate
UK cybersecurity chief Richard Horn warns of AI-linked breaches on critical infrastructure by 2028
Chicago entrepreneur Russell Steinberg turns empty downtown office space into indoor greens farm
Military says it rescued crew of Iranian fishing vessel hijacked off Somalia, with no casualties
